narrative:
Your loan application was carefully reviewed, and the assessment found a 58% likelihood that you represent a credit risk — a figure that, while not overwhelming, was sufficient to result in a denial. This decision was shaped primarily by three aspects of your financial profile: the current state of your checking account, the length of the loan you requested, and your credit history.

The single most influential factor working against your application was the status of your checking account, which currently carries a negative balance. Among applicants who were approved, only about one in five had a checking account in the red, and having a negative balance signals to the assessment that your day-to-day finances may already be under strain — making it harder to take on additional debt responsibly.

Closely behind that, the duration of the loan you requested raised significant concern. You applied for a 42-month credit term, more than double the average of roughly 19 months seen among approved applicants. A longer repayment period increases the uncertainty around whether financial circumstances will remain stable enough to meet obligations over time, and this extended timeline pushed the assessment meaningfully toward a denial.

On a more positive note, your credit history — classified as "critical/other credits" — actually worked slightly in your favor. While this category is not the strongest possible history, it is common among approved applicants, with about 35% of those who were approved sharing a similar background. This factor nudged the assessment modestly toward a more favorable view of your application, though it was not enough to outweigh the other concerns.

Beyond these top three factors, several other elements of your profile added to the overall picture of risk: you are currently unemployed, which is quite rare among approved applicants (fewer than 5% were in the same situation), and your installment rate of 4% of disposable income is higher than the approved applicant average of around 3%, meaning repayments would consume a larger share of your available funds. The loan purpose — home repairs — is also among the least common reasons for approved loans, representing under 2% of approvals.

As a next step, it would be worth focusing on stabilizing your checking account balance and, if possible, securing some form of employment before reapplying. You might also consider requesting a shorter loan term or a smaller amount, as both would reduce the perceived risk. Speaking directly with a bank advisor could help you understand what specific improvements would make the strongest difference in a future application.
